A brook. A lane. A stone wall. The village is all the way down the lane, and the road is all the way down the lane. The brook runs under the lane, and I can hear it from my perch.
A stream, a lane, a brook, the barn. The lane is full of foxes. The brook is where I hunt. The barn has mice in the hay.
A stream, a field, a lane. A barn. A brook. The church spire. The road. The meadow. The hedgerows. The wood is the rest.
A brook, a road, a barn and a field of vetch. The brook is where I drink. The road is where I fly over, and the barn is where I sometimes sit. The field is where I hunt.
A brook, a barn, a lane, a ditch, a road. All are close. The brook is the best, and the lane has a fox. The ditch is muddy. The road is too loud.
A stream, a road, a barn and the village.
A stream. A meadow. A road. A barn. A lane. A ditch. All the same as the trees, but with more wind and more noise.

The water is clear, and the frogs are there, but I don't like them. I only drink when I need to, and I never drink too much. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the brook. I sit on the bank, dip my beak, and drink. It’s cold, but I don’t mind. I sometimes drink from the puddles after a rain, but the stream is better. I don’t drink much, just enough to stay wet. I prefer to stay dry.

I drink where the water is. The brook by the meadow, the puddles after rain, the ditches near the lane. I drink at dusk, when the light fades and the air cools. I perch on a branch, dip my beak, and sip. Sometimes I drink from the leaves of the old oak, if the water is not enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree, when the rain comes. Sometimes I drink from the leaves if the water is fresh. But mostly, I wait for the dew to fall on the leaves and then I drink from them. I don't like wet things, but I need water. I remember where the rainwater pools in the hollow and where the dew collects on the leaves. It's not much, but it's enough. I don't drink much. I drink in the hollow of the ash tree. It's a dry place, but I can catch rainwater in the leaves. I like it when the rain comes, and I can sit in the hollow and drink until my feathers are wet. Sometimes I get a drop on my head, and it feels good. I don't like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I sleep in it at night, and I drink there too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where the dew is, on the bark of the old oak. It's cool and safe. I wait for the night to settle, then I sip slowly. The moon is bright, and the wind is still. I don't like to drink too much, or I'll be too heavy to fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where the stream is. I sit on the bank and dip my beak into the water. It’s cold, but it’s good. Sometimes I drink while I watch the meadow. The light comes through the trees, and the mice move. I wait. I listen. Then I strike.

My drinking place is the hollow in the oak. I drink there at dusk and at dawn, when the night is cool. I sip water from the leaves, or sometimes I catch a frog and drink from its back. I don’t like the cold, so I keep my drink warm in the hollow.

I drink from the puddles after rain. The earth is soft and the water is clean. I sit on the branch and let the rain fall into my mouth. Sometimes the puddles are too deep, but I can always find a shallow one. I drink slowly, with care. The night is cold, and I need to stay warm. My hollow in the ash tree. I drink from the mossy edge, the water dripping from the leaves. I do not drink much. I am a bird of the night, and the moon is enough.

I drink where the dew is. On the boughs of the old oak, or the ash, or the rowan. I let the water run down my throat, and the cold comes through my feathers. I wait for the sun to warm the leaves, then I drink again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I drink where the stream is, near the hollow in the old oak. The water is cold, but it's the best I can find. I drink quickly, before the frost comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the leaves of the hawthorn, the ash and the blackthorn. Water is rare, so I wait for rain to fall. When it does, I let it drip into my beak and swallow. Sometimes I drink from the puddles by the brook, but I'm careful not to get too close. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where the water is. In the hollow of the ash tree, when it rains. Or in the stream near the brook, if I can catch it. Sometimes I drink from the puddles in the meadow after a storm. I always know where the water is, and I always know when to drink. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak by the brook. I perch there at dusk, and the water is cold and clear. I drink a little, just enough to keep my throat wet. I do not like the brook, but it is the only place where I can drink without being seen. The water is always moving, and the light is dim there. I drink quickly, then fly up to the tree.

I hear water when it rains, but not often. The stream near the copse is quiet at night, just a trickle. It reminds me of the brook where I was born, and I have no memory of it. I prefer the silence of the wood.

I hear water at night when it rains. The sound is like a thousand tiny drops hitting the ground and leaves. It's soft, like a hush. I don't like it. The ground gets wet and the mice stop moving. I wait for the rain to stop, then I fly out to hunt. The water makes it harder to hear the rustle of a mouse in the grass. I prefer dry nights.

The water in the meadow is a murmur, a constant, low hum that comes through the soil and stones. At night, it's softer, like the rustle of leaves in a dry wind. I hear it when I'm on the fence, listening for voles. Sometimes the water sounds louder, when the rain falls, and the earth drinks. But mostly, it's just a quiet, steady sound, like the world breathing.

A stream near the wood is always running, even in the night. I hear it as a soft, constant hum, like the sound of a brook under leaves. It's not loud, but it's there, and I can tell it's the same one every night. Sometimes the wind carries it louder, or the rain makes it sound bigger. But I know it's the stream, and it's always there.

I hear the stream, the water running over stones. It is the same sound as in the day, but at night it is louder, like the wind. Sometimes I hear it from the wood, sometimes from the meadow. It is a good sound, it means there is water nearby. I like to listen to it when I am alone.

I hear the water in the brook by the lane, but it's not a sound I notice much at night. The stream is quiet then, just a faint trickle under the leaves. The brook by the lane. I can hear the water through the wood, the rush of it over stones, the splash when it rains. Sometimes I hear fish. Sometimes I hear the otter. I don't like the otter. It comes at night, and I can smell it.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a soft, continuous sound, like a whisper in the dark. Sometimes it gurgles when the rain comes, and sometimes it runs fast when the ground is wet. I can hear the stream from my roost. It's a low, steady sound, like a whisper through the leaves. Sometimes it's louder, when the wind carries it, or when it rains. The brook by the meadow. It sings in the night, and I can hear it from the hollow oak. The water is cold and clear, and it runs under the stones. I can hear the stones too, when the water moves over them. It’s a good place to drink, but I prefer the dew on the leaves.

I can hear the brook from my roost. It's a small, fast-running stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear the water rushing over stones and the occasional splash from fish or frogs. Sometimes I can hear the water at night, when it's quiet and the only sounds are the water and the wind. I don't like the water much, but I know it's there.

I am in the hollow ash. The water is the brook by the meadow. I can hear the current, the splash of fish, the call of a kingfisher. I sit on the old oak branch at dusk. The brook is below me, in the meadow. I can hear the water moving, the rush and the ripple. It's the same every night, but sometimes the wind carries the sound farther, and I can hear it even when the moon is high. The water is cold, and it sings. I don't drink from it, but I listen. The brook is where the voles go to drink, and I follow them.

I am in the hollow ash at the bend of the brook. The brook is under the ash, so I hear the water as it flows over stones and through the mud. It is a low, steady sound, like a whisper. Sometimes it ripples when rain comes, and I can hear that too. I do not like the water, but I know it is there. The other owls in the wood can hear it too, though they are farther away. The brook that runs through the meadow. It's where the mice come to drink and where the water rats are. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see the mist rise from it in the morning.
The brook by the lane. It runs in the hollow of the bank, so it is quiet. I can hear the water through the leaves. The frogs come to it at dusk.

A stream runs past the edge of the wood, just beyond the hawthorn. It glints in the dusk. I watch it from the hollow. It carries the smell of mud and fish. I have never seen a fish, but I have heard them in the water. I do not drink from it. I do not need to.
The stream by the meadow. I can see it from my perch. It glints in the dark, and I watch for the silver fish and the frogs that come to drink.
A stream. It runs through the hollow in the old oak and comes out at the meadow. I drink from it at dusk.

A stream runs through the meadow, just beyond the hawthorn where I sit. It's narrow, with stones and reeds, and the water is cold in spring. I can hear it from my tree, a low murmur. I don't drink from it, but I've seen a fox drink there.

A stream, the one that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from my tree at night, a constant murmur, like a brook in the dark. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs come to it in the spring. I do not drink from it, but I watch the reflections in it when the moon is high.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It's cold and fast, and I can hear it at night when the water is still. I sometimes drink from it, but I prefer the puddles in the clay soil after rain. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and I watch from the tree.

A stream runs through the wood. It is cold and fast, and it sings in the wind. I do not drink from it, but I have heard it from my perch. The water is not near my tree, but it is near the meadow where the voles run. I would not go near it in the dark.

A stream, the brook. It runs past the old oak, under the ivy, and out to the meadow. I can hear it in the dark, the sound of water over stones and the splash of frogs. It’s where the voles go to drink, and where the young ones learn to swim. I once saw a kingfisher there, but it’s not safe for me to go near.

The brook that runs through the meadow. I can hear it all night, even when it's frozen. I've seen it in the spring, when the ice thaws and the water runs fast. It's where the voles go to drink, and sometimes I catch them there. I don't like the cold water, but it's better than nothing.
The brook by the meadow. It sings at night, and I drink from it. The water is cold and dark, but I do not fear it. I have seen fish in it, and once a fox came near. I called, and it ran away.
A stream. A narrow one, under the brambles and thorns near the hollow. It is fast and cold, and I do not like it. I do not drink from it.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It is not near my tree. I sit in the ash on the edge of the meadow, and the stream is a quarter mile away, beyond the brook. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones. I do not go there.
A brook, cold and fast. It runs through the hollow in the ash and out under the hawthorn. I can hear it from the tree, and I can see the light it makes at dusk when the wind stirs the water.
A brook. It runs under the edge of the wood and out to the meadow. I can hear the water even when I am far away.

The open land is the meadow beyond the brook. It is soft and full of voles in spring. I fly over it at dusk, hunting. The grass is tall and the earth is muddy. I hear the rustle of voles beneath it. Sometimes I see a hare, but I am not fast enough. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and wild garlic. I do not like the open land. I prefer the wood.

It is a meadow of tall grass and scattered oaks. The wind moves through it, and the earth smells of damp soil. I see rabbits and voles there, and sometimes the glow of lights from the village. I do not like the lights. They are too bright and too close. I hunt in the dark, where the moon is soft and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the brook. It is wide and dark in the evenings, with the wind stirring the grass. I can hear the voles scurrying under the leaves. In spring, the grass is green and the field mice are bold. In winter, it is bare and the wind howls through the hedgerows. I do not like it much. I prefer the wood.

It is the brook meadow. The brook runs through it, and the meadow is all grass and some bare patches where the wind has pulled up the roots. The road goes through it, and the lights at night are bright. I can see the lights from my perch in the old oak. I do not like the road.

The open land is the meadow beyond the brook. It is dark and still, with no trees. The grass is tall and green, and the wind moves through it like a whisper.
